left.heading: An object becomes evidence.
left.introduction: Before astronauts arrived, robotic scouts tested the Moon. Surveyor 3 photographed its surroundings and examined the soil. Two years later, Apollo 12 astronauts returned parts of the lander to Earth. The machine itself had become an experiment.
left.question: Can a machine teach us something after it stops transmitting?

left.heading: The camera that became evidence
left.intro: After about 2½ years on the Moon, the television camera returned to Earth. Engineers examined its optics, electronics, mechanisms, materials and coatings.
left.question: Which record would help you evaluate a material’s performance: a landing photograph, or tests of the returned hardware?

right.pipelineText: Camera → observe the Moon → returned by Apollo 12 → test how materials and instruments endured lunar exposure.

left.heading: An object becomes evidence.

left.heading: Seven minutes of terror
left.intro: Landing was a sequence of different engineering jobs. Follow what each piece of equipment did, and why it was left behind.

rightSteps.title: Atmospheric entry
rightSteps.purpose: Protect the rover from intense entry heating.
rightSteps.fate: The heat shield separates later, once its protective job is done.
rightSteps.touchdownCaption: Earth received touchdown at 05:31:45.4 UTC, about 13m48s later. Event occurrence and Earth reception are different times.

rightSteps.title: Parachute deployment
rightSteps.purpose: Use the atmosphere to slow the descending spacecraft.
rightSteps.fate: The back shell and parachute are later discarded before powered descent.
rightSteps.touchdownCaption: Earth received touchdown at 05:31:45.4 UTC, about 13m48s later. Event occurrence and Earth reception are different times.

rightSteps.title: Heat-shield separation
rightSteps.purpose: Clear the view for landing sensors after protection is no longer needed.
rightSteps.fate: The shield falls separately to the surface.
rightSteps.touchdownCaption: Earth received touchdown at 05:31:45.4 UTC, about 13m48s later. Event occurrence and Earth reception are different times.

rightSteps.time: Ordered stage · exact time not specified here
rightSteps.title: Back shell separates
rightSteps.purpose: Release the powered descent stage and rover for controlled descent.
rightSteps.fate: The back shell and attached parachute land separately. This is not rover separation.
rightSteps.touchdownCaption: Earth received touchdown at 05:31:45.4 UTC, about 13m48s later. Event occurrence and Earth reception are different times.

rightSteps.title: Rover separation
rightSteps.purpose: Lower the rover below the powered descent stage on tethers.
rightSteps.fate: The stage continues controlling descent while the rover approaches the ground.
rightSteps.touchdownCaption: Earth received touchdown at 05:31:45.4 UTC, about 13m48s later. Event occurrence and Earth reception are different times.

rightSteps.title: Touchdown
rightSteps.purpose: Place the laboratory on its wheels, ready for surface operations.
rightSteps.fate: Tethers are cut; the powered descent stage flies away and impacts separately.
rightSteps.touchdownCaption: Earth received touchdown at 05:31:45.4 UTC, about 13m48s later. Event occurrence and Earth reception are different times.

left.heading: An object becomes evidence.
left.introduction: Launched in 1972, Pioneer 10 became the first spacecraft to fly past Jupiter. Its last signal reached Earth in January 2003. The hardware continues on its outward journey, while the observations it returned remain part of humanity’s scientific record.
left.question: What remains when a spacecraft can no longer call home?

left.heading: The 11-hour message
left.intro: NASA received Pioneer 10’s last faint signal with no telemetry. At about 12.23 billion km away, its signal needed about 11 hours 20 minutes to reach Earth.
left.note: Controllers plan ahead. They cannot use a live steering wheel across this distance.
